concepts.title: Electric Current as Charge Flow Rate
concepts.definition: Current through a cross-section is the net charge crossing it in the forward sense divided by the time taken, with the sign telling which way it runs.
concepts.key_idea: Steady current means this quotient stays constant; the ampere is the SI unit and lightning reaches tens of thousands of them.
question_patterns: a charge of 90 coulomb crosses a wire section in one minute; find the current
how much charge flows through a conductor carrying 2 ampere for 10 seconds
calculate the current when a stated charge passes a cross-section in a given time
find the flow rate of charge through a bulb from the charge moved and the time taken
the net charge across a section is 0.5 coulomb each second; what current does that make

solution_steps.action: split the charge by the elapsed time
solution_steps.explain: current is defined as the charge transported per unit time through the section

concepts.title: Ohm Law and Resistance
concepts.definition: For ohmic conductors the drop across the ends grows in direct proportion to the current, and the fixed ratio of drop to current defines the resistance in ohms.
concepts.key_idea: The proportionality V with I is the physical claim of the law; the ratio R can be quoted for any conductor, ohmic or not.
question_patterns: a drop of 6 volt drives 2 ampere through a resistor; find its resistance
determine the resistance of a conductor from the voltage across it and the current through it
what does the ratio of potential difference to current give for a metallic wire
a heater draws 4 ampere on a 220 volt line; compute the element resistance
state the relation between voltage and current for materials that follow the linear law

solution_steps.action: divide the drop by the current
solution_steps.explain: resistance is the constant ratio of the potential difference across a conductor to the current it carries

compute_steps.action: substitute the given values into the formula

concepts.title: Resistance from Resistivity and Geometry
concepts.definition: A wire opposes current in proportion to its length and in inverse proportion to its cross-sectional area, with the material constant rho setting the scale.
concepts.key_idea: Resistivity belongs to the material and ignores its shape; stretching a wire longer and thinner multiplies its resistance twice over.
question_patterns: a wire 15 m long with cross-section 6 times 10 to the minus 7 metre squared measures 5 ohm; find the material resistivity
find the resistance of a wire of given length, area and resistivity
calculate R for a conductor using rho l over A with numbers
how does the resistance of a wire respond when its length is doubled and the area kept fixed
compute the resistance of a rod of stated material and dimensions

solution_steps.action: form the length to area ratio
solution_steps.explain: geometry enters only through length divided by cross-sectional area
multiplying the geometry ratio by the resistivity completes the resistance

concepts.title: Drift Speed of Conduction Electrons
concepts.definition: Electrons in a current-carrying metal crawl along with a small average speed set by the current divided by the carrier charge, density and area, while their random thermal motion stays far faster.
concepts.key_idea: Drift is slow, about a millimetre per second, yet the field that starts it travels at light speed, so lamps glow at once.
question_patterns: estimate how fast conduction electrons drift along a copper wire of given area carrying 1.5 ampere
find v d for a metal wire from the current, carrier density, electronic charge and cross-section

compute the average drift velocity of free electrons using n, e, A and I
compare the drift speed of electrons in a wire with their random thermal speed

solution_steps.explain: each carrier carries e = 1.6e-19 C

solution_steps.action: divide the current by the carrier flow factors
solution_steps.explain: current equals n e A v d, so the drift speed is the current split by density, charge and area together

concepts.title: Mobility of Charge Carriers
concepts.definition: Mobility measures how easily carriers respond to a field, quoted as the drift speed gained per unit field strength, with units of metre squared per volt second.
concepts.key_idea: Mobility equals e tau over m, linking collision time to conduction quality; it is always taken positive.
question_patterns: find the mobility of carriers whose drift speed is 1 millimetre per second inside a field of 100 volt per metre
define mobility and give its SI unit
calculate the mobility from a stated drift velocity and applied field
how is mobility related to the relaxation time of electron collisions
a carrier gains 0.5 millimetre per second of drift per 50 volt per metre; what is its mobility

solution_steps.action: split the drift speed by the field
solution_steps.explain: mobility is defined as the drift velocity obtained per unit electric field

concepts.title: Where Ohm Law Fails
concepts.definition: Some devices break the proportionality between drop and current: the graph bends, the answer flips when the polarity reverses, or one current admits several voltages, as in diodes and GaAs.
concepts.key_idea: Ohm law is a material behaviour, not a law of nature; V equals I times R still defines resistance even for non-ohmic devices.
question_patterns: name the ways a device can fail to follow the linear voltage current law
why does a junction diode not obey the proportionality of voltage and current
give an example of a material where one current corresponds to more than one voltage
does reversing the polarity always reverse the current equally in every device
is the linear voltage current relation a fundamental law of nature

solution_steps.explain: the law holds only while the voltage current plot stays a straight line through the origin
some devices pass different currents for plus and minus V of equal size, diodes being the standard case
materials such as GaAs allow several voltages for one current, breaking the law in a third way

concepts.title: Temperature Dependence of Resistance
concepts.definition: Near a reference temperature a metal resistance grows linearly with temperature, the fractional rise per degree being the temperature coefficient alpha.
concepts.key_idea: Metals carry a positive alpha while semiconductors fall in resistance as they warm, because their carrier count grows faster than collisions shorten tau.
question_patterns: a heating element reads 100 ohm at 27 degrees and 117 ohm when hot; find its temperature given alpha 1.7 times 10 to the minus 4
calculate the resistance of a platinum wire at a stated temperature from its ice point value and alpha
find the rise in temperature of a nichrome element from its cold and hot resistance values
how does the resistance of a metal change when its temperature rises by a given amount
a silver wire shows 2.1 ohm and 2.7 ohm at two temperatures; work out the temperature coefficient

solution_steps.explain: the linear law uses the excess of the working temperature over the reference temperature
multiply the reference resistance by one plus alpha times the rise

concepts.title: Material Classes by Resistivity
concepts.definition: Materials sort by resistivity into metals near 10 to the minus 8 ohm metre, insulators up to 10 to the 18 times larger, and semiconductors between, whose resistivity drops on heating and shrinks further with doping.
concepts.key_idea: Only semiconductors combine a mid-range resistivity with strong temperature and impurity sensitivity, the basis of electronic devices.
question_patterns: arrange metals, semiconductors and insulators by their resistivity ranges
why are semiconductors preferred for electronic devices over metals
roughly how many times larger is the resistivity of an insulator than that of a metal
which class of materials shows falling resistivity as temperature rises
what role do added impurities play in the resistivity of a semiconductor

solution_steps.explain: metal resistivities sit around 10 to the minus 8 ohm metre, semiconductors in the middle band, insulators astronomically higher
metals warm upward in resistivity, semiconductors fall as heat frees more carriers
trace impurities pull semiconductor resistivity down by orders of magnitude, which is what device engineering exploits

concepts.title: Ohmic Power Dissipation
concepts.definition: A resistor turns electrical energy into heat at the rate of the current squared times its resistance, which is why transmission lines are run at enormous voltages to keep losses small.
concepts.key_idea: The same loss reads V times I or V squared over R; the I squared R form explains why cutting the current pays off quadratically in transmission.
question_patterns: a bulb filament of 10 ohm carries 3 ampere; compute its power dissipation through heating
calculate the heat produced per second in a resistor from its current and resistance

solution_steps.action: square the current into the resistance
solution_steps.explain: the dissipation rate equals the current squared multiplied by the resistance

concepts.title: Current from a Cell with Internal Resistance
concepts.definition: A real cell drives the circuit with its emf while its own internal resistance shares the load, so the current is the emf split between the outside resistance and the inside one together.
concepts.key_idea: Short-circuiting the cell gives the largest possible current, emf over r, which real cells are never allowed to deliver.

solution_steps.action: split the emf over the total

concepts.title: Terminal Voltage of a Real Cell
concepts.definition: The voltage available at the terminals sits below the emf by the internal drop, the product of the drawn current and the internal resistance.
concepts.key_idea: Open circuit reads the full emf; heavier loading drags the terminal voltage down until charging current would push it above emf.

solution_steps.explain: the emf loses I times r inside the cell before reaching the terminals

concepts.title: Cells in Series Driving a Load
concepts.definition: Cells stacked in series contribute their emfs (signs honoured) and their internal resistances, both by plain addition, before the usual current rule is applied.
concepts.key_idea: A cell turned the wrong way subtracts its emf; the internal resistances always add regardless of orientation.

solution_steps.explain: matching orientations add; a reversed cell enters with a minus sign

concepts.title: Kirchhoff Junction and Loop Rules
concepts.definition: Circuit analysis rests on two bookkeeping rules: charge counted per second into a junction equals charge out, and walking any closed loop of a circuit returns the potential to its starting value.
concepts.key_idea: The junction rule is charge conservation, the loop rule is energy conservation; together they solve any network, however tangled.

solution_steps.explain: label branch currents with arrows; at every node, incoming currents sum to outgoing ones
walk each closed mesh adding signed voltage changes across cells and resistors until the total is zero
enough independent junction and loop equations determine every unknown branch current

concepts.title: Wheatstone Bridge Balance Condition
concepts.definition: In a four-arm bridge fed across one diagonal, the galvanometer across the other diagonal reads zero exactly when the products of opposite arms match, or equivalently the two arm ratios agree.
concepts.key_idea: At balance no current crosses the bridge arm, the junction and loop rules collapse to the ratio condition, and one unknown arm becomes measurable.
question_patterns: state the condition for zero deflection in a Wheatstone bridge
when does the galvanometer of a balanced bridge carry no current
for four bridge arms in ratio, write the balance equation among R1 R2 R3 R4

how does a balanced bridge help measure an unknown resistance

solution_steps.explain: zero galvanometer current forces equal junction pairings I1 = I3 and I2 = I4
the meshes through the galvanometer then demand equal drops across the upper and lower arms
combining the loops gives the product-of-opposites rule that defines balance

concepts.title: Unknown Resistance from a Balanced Bridge
concepts.definition: Once the bridge is balanced, the fourth arm follows from the other three, since the arm products of opposite sides must agree.
concepts.key_idea: Adjust one known arm until the galvanometer falls silent, then the unknown is a single multiplication away; the meter bridge works this way.
question_patterns: three arms of a balanced bridge read 10, 60 and 5 ohm; find the fourth arm
find the unknown resistance in a Wheatstone bridge when the other three arms are known at balance
a meter bridge is balanced; compute the unknown from the remaining arms
use the balance condition to evaluate the missing resistance of a bridge
given R1, R2 and R3 of a null bridge, determine R4

solution_steps.explain: at balance the product of one diagonal pair equals that of the other
splitting that product by the first known arm leaves the unknown fourth resistance
